1.title: Agent Architecture and Patterns
1.text: Welcome to Module five: Agent Architecture and Patterns. This module covers the skills agent architecture, agent patterns and frameworks. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Workflow versus agent: the decision criteria. Manager and supervisor hierarchies and the role of subagents. The common agent patterns: tool-use loop, subagents, memory, context-window management. The common workflow patterns: chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer. Agentic frameworks (Strands, Lang Graph, Pydantic A I) and when to use one.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater Automates Claim Intake
1.text: Our running case is Tidewater Insurance. Tidewater Automates Claim Intake. Step list today: read the claim email, extract the policy number, check coverage, draft a reply. Some claims are odd: missing data, several policies, unclear damage. The team asks: "Do we need an agent, or just a workflow?".

1.title: Workflow or Agent?
1.text: Workflow or Agent? Control. Workflow: Your code defines the path (fixed or branching steps). Agent: The model decides the next step in a loop with tools. Predictability. Workflow: High: same steps, testable, cheaper. Agent: Lower: flexible, harder to test. Fits. Workflow: Well-understood tasks with known steps. Agent: Open-ended tasks where the steps depend on what is found. Cost and latency. Workflow: Lower, bounded. Agent: Higher, variable (many model calls).

1.title: Workflow or Agent?, continued
1.text: Workflow or Agent?, continued. The figure shows this: Start simple: a single call if it is enough, a workflow if the steps are known, an agent only when the path depends on what the task reveals. Decision criteria: predictability of the steps, complexity, cost and latency budget, tolerance for errors, and need for auditing. Start with the simplest thing that works: one good prompt, then a workflow, then an agent. Add autonomy only when the simpler design fails the evals.

1.title: Workflow or Agent?, continued
1.text: Workflow or Agent?, continued. Many real systems are workflows with one agentic step (for example a fixed intake pipeline that hands odd cases to an agent). Exam tip: "Steps are known and must be reliable and cheap" to workflow. "The path depends on what the task discovers" to agent.

1.title: Workflow Patterns
1.text: Workflow Patterns. The figure shows this: Five workflow patterns: chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers and evaluator-optimizer.

1.title: Workflow Patterns, continued
1.text: Workflow Patterns, continued. Prompt chaining. Use it when: A task splits into fixed sequential steps. Claims example: Extract fields, then check coverage, then draft the reply. Routing. Use it when: Inputs fall into categories that need different handling. Claims example: Route "auto" and "property" claims to different prompts or models. Parallelization. Use it when: Independent subtasks, or the same task several times for confidence. Claims example: Review ten documents at once; vote on a coverage decision. Orchestrator-workers. Use it when: The subtasks cannot be predicted in advance. Claims example: A planner splits a large claim file into parts for workers.

1.title: Workflow Patterns, continued
1.text: Workflow Patterns, continued. Evaluator-optimizer. Use it when: A clear quality criterion exists and iteration improves the result. Claims example: Draft a reply, critique it against a checklist, revise. Exam tip: A fixed pipeline with one hard case is usually a workflow with an agentic step, not a fully autonomous agent.

1.title: Agent Architecture: Loops, Supervisors and Subagents
1.text: Agent Architecture: Loops, Supervisors and Subagents. Tool-use loop (the core agent pattern): send the request, the model returns tool use, your code runs the tool and returns the result, repeat until end turn (see the loop in the Architect course; here it is a pattern to recognize). Manager or supervisor hierarchy: a supervisor agent breaks a goal into tasks, delegates to subagents, collects results and decides what is next.

1.title: Agent Architecture: Loops, Supervisors and Subagents, continued
1.text: Agent Architecture: Loops, Supervisors and Subagents, continued. Why subagents improve task execution:; Context isolation: verbose work stays in the subagent's own context window; only a summary returns; Specialization: a focused prompt and a small tool set per role; Parallelism: independent subagents run at the same time. Memory: short-term is the conversation in the context window; long-term is stored outside the model (files, a database, a memory tool) and loaded when relevant. Context-window management: prune tool output, summarize or compact, delegate to subagents (Module nine).

1.title: Agent Architecture: Loops, Supervisors and Subagents, continued
1.text: Agent Architecture: Loops, Supervisors and Subagents, continued. The figure shows this: A supervisor delegates to specialist subagents with isolated context; summaries return; long-term memory lives outside the context window.

1.title: Agentic Frameworks
1.text: Agentic Frameworks. Claude Agent S D K (software development kit). What it is: The agent loop and tools behind Claude Code, as a library. Typical reason to choose it: You want Claude's own harness: tools, subagents, hooks, sessions. Strands Agents. What it is: A model-driven agent framework (strong A W S integration). Typical reason to choose it: Building agents with tools on A W S with little code. Lang Graph. What it is: Stateful graphs of nodes and edges for multi-step workflows. Typical reason to choose it: Explicit control flow, branching, persistence and human-in-the-loop steps. Pydantic A I. What it is: An agent framework built around typed, validated outputs (Pydantic models). Typical reason to choose it: Strongly typed structured outputs and validation.

1.title: Agentic Frameworks, continued
1.text: Agentic Frameworks, continued. Framework or direct A P I (application programming interface)? A framework gives faster development, patterns and state handling; the cost is abstraction (you see less of the prompts and calls), extra dependencies and the need to understand what runs underneath. Use the plain A P I for simple flows and when you need full control. Whatever you pick, you still need evals, logging and guardrails; a framework does not replace them. Exam tip: Pick a framework for the specific capability it offers (state graph, typed output, Claude's own harness); do not pick one just because it is popular.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Workflow versus agent: Workflow equals your code sets the path; agent equals the model decides in a loop. Choose: Known steps to workflow; open-ended to agent; start simple. Workflow patterns: Chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer. Subagents: Context isolation, specialization, parallelism; summaries return. Memory: Short-term equals context window; long-term equals external store. Frameworks: Claude Agent S D K, Strands, Lang Graph (stateful graphs), Pydantic A I (typed outputs). Framework tradeoff: Speed and patterns versus abstraction and dependencies; evals still required.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. The steps of Tidewater's invoice check are always the same: extract fields, validate totals, write a summary. Reliability and low cost matter. What fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Known, fixed steps call for a workflow, which is more predictable and cheaper than an agent.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. An investigation task has no fixed steps: what to check next depends on what the previous check found. Which design suits it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. When the path depends on discoveries, the model must choose the next step.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Incoming claims fall into auto, property and liability categories, each needing a different prompt. Which pattern fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Routing sends inputs of different types to specialized handling.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A developer wants an answer drafted, then critiqued against a checklist and revised until it passes. Which pattern is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Generate, evaluate against criteria, and iterate is the evaluator-optimizer pattern.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A large claim file must be split into parts that cannot be known ahead of time, each handled by a worker. Which pattern is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. An orchestrator plans dynamic subtasks and delegates them to workers.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Why use subagents in a supervisor design? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Isolation, specialization and parallelism improve task execution and keep the supervisor's context small.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. An agent must remember customer preferences across many sessions. What is the right place for long-term memory? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Context windows are per request; durable memory belongs in external storage.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. A team needs explicit state, branching and human approval steps in a multi-step workflow. Which kind of framework fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Stateful graph frameworks model nodes, edges and persisted state explicitly.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. Select two. Which two are good reasons to prefer the plain A P I over a framework? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and D. Simple flows and a small dependency footprint favor the plain A P I; frameworks do not remove the need for evals or guarantee correctness.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all nine answers. Question one: D. Question two: D. Question three: A. Question four: C. Question five: B. Question six: B. Question seven: B. Question eight: C. Question nine: A and D. In the next module, we continue the course.
